read.bigIdea: Porter was the first industrial beer.
read.where: Porter grew out of London “**brown beer**” in the **1700s** and was first prized aged. The stories that Ralph Harwood invented it in 1722 and that it was named after market porters have little evidence. It was arguably the first **mass-produced** beer and peaked in the **1820s**; brewers installed **steam engines** early. In **1817** Daniel Wheeler’s **black patent malt** let brewers make porter mostly from pale malt. Whitbread brewed its last porter in 1940.
read.mixup: The “porters drank it, so it’s called porter” story is probably a legend.

video.title: The true history of the IPA | The Craft Beer Channel

read.bigIdea: Two revolutions: pale ale, then cold.
read.where: William **Bass** founded his Burton-on-Trent brewery in **1777**; its **red triangle** became the UK’s first registered trademark in **1876**. “Lager” comes from the German **lagern**, to store: from 1553 Bavaria banned summer brewing, so brewers stored beer in cold cellars on lake ice. In **1873** Carl von **Linde**’s first practical refrigeration went into Munich’s **Spaten** brewery, and lager could be brewed anywhere, any season. Today about **9 in 10** beers drunk worldwide are lagers.
read.mixup: Lager isn’t a modern style. Cold storage goes back centuries; refrigeration just spread it.

video.title: Documentaries and Specials | Prohibition Extra | Survival of the Breweries

read.bigIdea: America’s beer rose, crashed and consolidated.
read.where: In **1840** John Wagner brought Bavarian **lager yeast** to Philadelphia, and German immigrants spread it. The US peaked at **4,131 breweries** in **1873**, a number not passed again until **2015**. **Prohibition** took effect in **1920**; the 21st Amendment ended it in **December 1933**. Then came consolidation: by **1978** there were just **89 breweries**, owned by fewer than 50 companies.
read.mixup: Beer came back before full repeal: 3.2% beer was allowed in spring 1933.

video.title: How Jimmy Carter Jump-Started the Craft Beer Revolution | WSJ

read.where: President Carter signed **H.R. 1337** on October 14, **1978**, making **homebrewing** federally legal; Charlie Papazian founded the American Homebrewers Association the same year. Fritz Maytag had already bought **Anchor** in San Francisco (1964 or 1965, sources differ), and Jack McAuliffe opened **New Albion** in Sonoma in **1976**, usually called the first modern microbrewery. The Brewers Association defines a **craft brewer** as **small** (6 million barrels a year or less) and **independent** (under 25% owned by a non-craft alcohol company). It counts **9,724** US breweries for 2025.
read.mixup: Craft isn’t about taste. It’s the BA’s definition by size and ownership, which is why some famous brands no longer count.
